defaultRowSpacingInches.publisher: Virginia Cooperative Extension (Virginia Tech / Virginia State University)
defaultRowSpacingInches.quote: VCE 426-331, Virginia’s Home Garden Vegetable Planting Guide, Table 5 (Crop | Distance between plants in row | Distance between rows): "Squash, winter | 2-4 ft | 3-10 ft"
defaultRowSpacingInches.note: Lower end of VCE’s between-row range, feet converted to inches, per #591 ruling Q1 (3-0); VCE: "How wide you space the rows depends on the dimensions of the garden beds and the size of the hand tools or power tools used to control weeds between rows."

keepApart.publisher: University of Wisconsin-Madison Division of Extension, Garden Facts XHT1132 (David M. Lowenstein and Russell L. Groves, "Potato Leafhopper")
keepApart.quote: Avoid planting sensitive crops near alfalfa fields , because PLHs will migrate from alfalfa to these crops when the alfalfa field is harvested.
keepApart.note: The same fact sheet names the sensitive crops: "Snap beans and potatoes should be monitored regularly for PLH activity , especially in early summer after alfalfa is cut." Only snap bean (Phaseolus vulgaris pod bean) and potato plugins are listed; other PLH hosts the sheet mentions (eggplant, strawberry, apple) are not tied to the alfalfa advice there. Michigan State Extension E-2269 (1992) agrees for dry beans: "Be sure to check dry bean fields after nearby alfalfa fields are cut because cutting causes the adult leafhoppers to leave alfalfa fields." The spacing before "PLH" and "," is as extracted from the PDF text.

seedingRate.drillRowSpacingIn.publisher: Virginia Cooperative Extension, Agronomy Handbook 2023 (424-100), Part I, Alfalfa
seedingRate.drillRowSpacingIn.quote: Method of planting 6-8 inch rows or solid-seeded.
seedingRate.drillRowSpacingIn.note: The drilled rate comes from Missouri G4652; broadcast is empty because Missouri gives only a ceiling (up to 20).

seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.publisher: University of Missouri Extension G4652, Seeding Rates, Dates and Depths for Common Missouri Forages (Harley D. Naumann)
seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.quote: Missouri G4652 Table 1. Pure stands, columns "Type | Seeding rate (pounds of live seed per acre) | Seeding date (Spring, Fall, Dormant or frost seeding) | Depth"; row "Alfalfa Perennial, warm-season legume Drilled: 12 – 15 Broadcast: Up to 20 Up to mid-April Late August – late September 1/4 – 1/2 inch"
seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.note: Forage pure-stand rate; the plugin is a hay alfalfa, so it counts. The only source that ties an alfalfa rate to a method: VCE 424-100 15-25, Penn State 15-18, Kentucky AGR-18 and Utah 15-20 name no method (panel ruling 2026-10-05, #551, 2-1). Broadcast stays empty: 'Up to 20' is a ceiling, not a range. 'Live seed' is not 'pure live seed', so no seedBasis.

seedingRate.seedBasis.quote: Rate. Recommended seeding rate for drilling and broadcasting a pure stand in lb./A, bu/A. and oz./100 sq. ft., assuming legal standards for germination percentage. Seeding rate will depend on the cover crop’s primary purpose and other factors.

seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.publisher: Virginia Cooperative Extension, Agronomy Handbook 2023 (424-100), Part I, Barley
seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.quote: Rate of seeding 120 lbs/A (hulled) or approximately 30 seeds/sq ft (18 seeds/drill foot in 7-inch rows) Method of planting Planting with a grain drill is best, but broadcast disk-in to a depth of 1-1 1/2 inches can be successful.

seasonalTasks.tip-primocanes.publisher: Virginia Cooperative Extension (Virginia Tech / Virginia State University)
seasonalTasks.tip-primocanes.quote: VCE 426-840, Small Fruit in the Home Garden: "Blackberry plants should be summer top pruned when the young shoots (primocanes) are about 5 feet tall."
seasonalTasks.tip-primocanes.note: OP-20 panel 2026-10-05 (docs/design/ORCHARD_CALENDAR.md, table "OP-20 number rulings"). Q5 (3-0): 4 ft had no source and is replaced by 5 ft. Agreeing semi-erect sources: Oregon State Extension ("tipped to about 3 feet (erect) or 5 feet (semi-erect)", on a page that names Triple Crown) and Missouri Extension G6000 ("summer tip them at 5 feet"). NC State and Missouri State train semi-erect canes to the top wire, which does not conflict.

defaultRowSpacingInches.publisher: Virginia Cooperative Extension (Virginia Tech / Virginia State University)
defaultRowSpacingInches.quote: VCE 426-840, Small Fruit in the Home Garden: "When planting in rows, allow at least 8 feet between rows to facilitate cultivation. Red and purple raspberries can be set 3 feet apart within the row; set erect and semierect blackberries plants 5 feet apart."
defaultRowSpacingInches.note: Feet converted to inches. Triple Crown is a semierect blackberry; Table 1 lists only erect (10 ft) and trailing (8 ft) blackberries, so the caneberry minimum in the text is used (#591 ruling Q4, 3-0).

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach (Yard and Garden)
inRowSpacingIn.quote: ISU Yard and Garden, Growing and Harvesting Ornamental Corn: "Ears vary from small (less than 6 inches in length) to large (6 to 12 inches long)."; "Bloody Butcher - heirloom cultivar; ears are 8 to 12 inches long; blood red kernels; can be ground into corn meal or flour."; "Space seeds 8 to 10 inches apart within rows for small-eared cultivars and 10 to 12 inches apart for large-eared cultivars."
inRowSpacingIn.note: Bloody Butcher is named in ISU's cultivar list with ears in the large (6-12 in) class, so the large-eared 10-12 in figure applies (small-eared is 8-10 in). Seed spacing at sowing; no thinning stated. Only one allowed source read. The existing Harris Seeds source (9-12 in) is a seed company and does not count.

harvestIndicators.quote: Cornell Vegetable Growing Guide, Corn: "choose another type of corn that you won’t harvest until the ears are fully mature and dry. These include popcorn, ornamental corn or field corn (dent, flint and flour corns grown for meal or animal feed)."

rowSpacingIn.publisher: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach (Yard and Garden)
rowSpacingIn.quote: ISU Extension, Growing and Harvesting Ornamental Corn: "Space seeds 8 to 10 inches apart within rows for small-eared cultivars and 10 to 12 inches apart for large-eared cultivars."; "Rows should be spaced 30 to 36 inches apart."

daysToMaturity.publisher: Virginia Cooperative Extension (Virginia Tech / Virginia State University)
daysToMaturity.quote: VCE 426-840, Small Fruit in the Home Garden: Table 1, Average bearing age (years): "Blueberry | 6 | 5 | 4-6 | 3 | 20-30"
daysToMaturity.note: Bearing age in years converted at 365 days/year, matching the existing perennial daysToMaturity convention (e.g. blueberry-duke-northern-highbush 1095). seasonalTasks.winter-prune.publisher: Virginia Cooperative Extension (Virginia Tech / Virginia State University)
seasonalTasks.winter-prune.quote: VCE 426-840, Small Fruit in the Home Garden: "Locate the oldest canes and prune out one of every six existing canes; cut as close to the ground as possible." Same page: "A mature blueberry bush should have 10 to 15 canes: two to three canes each of 1-, 2-, 3-, 4-, and 5-year-old canes (fig. 3)."
seasonalTasks.winter-prune.note: OP-20 panel 2026-10-05 (docs/design/ORCHARD_CALENDAR.md, table "OP-20 number rulings"). Q7 (3-0): one of every six kept in words, inside UVM Extension's "Up to one fifth of all canes can be removed per year" ceiling. Q8 (3-0): the unsourced 6-8 cane target is replaced by VCE's 10 to 15; Penn State gives 10 to 15, UVM 10 to 20 and 15 to 20, UMaine six to ten, all overlapping.

seasonalTasks.harvest.publisher: Virginia Cooperative Extension (Virginia Tech / Virginia State University)
seasonalTasks.harvest.quote: VCE 426-840, Small Fruit in the Home Garden: "Picking is usually necessary only once every five to seven days, more frequently if bird pressure is high."
seasonalTasks.harvest.note: OP-20 panel 2026-10-05 (docs/design/ORCHARD_CALENDAR.md, table "OP-20 number rulings"). Q9 (3-0): kept in words as VCE writes it; Mississippi State Extension P3801 agrees ("harvest every five to seven days").

harvestIndicators.publisher: Penn State Extension
harvestIndicators.quote: Penn State Extension, Cereal Rye as a Cover Crop: "Roll-crimping alone will not kill the cover crop until after anthesis (pollen shed), and if rolled-crimped before anthesis, it should be followed by a burndown spray." ... "It is not recommended to incorporate mature rye because soil microbes require a lot of N to break down high C:N rye, causing N deficiency in the next crop."

seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.publisher: SARE, Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Cereal Rye
seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.quote: Drill 60 to 120 lb./A (1 to 2 bushels) into a prepared seedbed or broadcast 90 to 160 lb./A (1.5 to 3 bushels) and disk lightly or cultipack (361, 422).
seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.note: Chart 3B agrees (drilled 60-120, broadcast 90-160). The NRCS Iowa / Iowa State cover crop fact sheets (May 2025) print lower single pure-live-seed rates (rye 45 drilled and 50 broadcast, mustard 3 and 4). Seed basis alone cannot close a two- to three-fold gap; they are Midwest Cover Crops Council baseline rates for Iowa corn and soybean systems, and the rye sheet says 'If grazing or weed suppression is desired, increase seeding rate.' A different purpose and region, so not counted (panel ruling 2026-10-04). Maryland NRCS 340 (2025) prints winter rye 90 and mustard 8, inside these ranges.

seedingRate.seedsPerAcre.publisher: Virginia Cooperative Extension, Agronomy Handbook 2023 (424-100), Part I, Corn
seedingRate.seedsPerAcre.quote: Rate of planting On soils with high production potential where good production practices are followed, plant 25,000 to 33,000 kernels per acre. If planted on droughty soils, the rate of planting should be decreased by 10%-15%.
seedingRate.seedsPerAcre.note: Single source (VCE). Kernels planted per acre on soils with high production potential; the same sentence lowers the rate 10-15% on droughty soils. Row width stays empty permanently unless a source changes (panel ruling 2026-10-05, 3-0): Iowa State's 'The most common row spacing for corn across the Corn Belt is 30 inches' and Nebraska G2216 describe practice, not a recommendation.

seedingRate.notRecorded.publisher: University of Maryland Extension FS-1134, No-Till Spring Vegetables After Forage Radish Cover Crop
seedingRate.notRecorded.quote: Recommended seeding rates for the popular Tillage Radish brand are 6 lbs/acre drilled, though research trials at the University of Maryland generally used a higher seeding rate of 8-9 lbs/acre. Broadcast rates are higher (9-12 lbs/acre), and germination from broadcast cover crop seed is greater when seed-soil contact is increased by cultipacking (crushing dirt clods, removing air pockets, and pressing down small stones to form a smooth, firm seedbed) or light incorporation.
seedingRate.notRecorded.note: Why both rates are empty (panel ruling 2026-10-05, #551, 3-0 drilled, 2-1 broadcast): drilled, the SARE page's 8-12 (Chart 3B 8-13, UW A4191 10-12, MD NRCS 340 8, Kentucky AGR-18 oilseed radish 10) does not overlap UMD's 6 or PA NRCS 340's 5. Broadcast, SARE's 12-20 shares only 12 with UMD's 9-12, and a single shared endpoint counts as a disagreement (as for orchardgrass). Ohio ANR-0125 (2-4/3-5 pure live seed) is an MCCC baseline and Virginia DCR SL-8B's 6-8 names no method. Penn State Agronomy Guide 2025 is paywalled and was not read.

seedingRate.sownBy.broadcast.note: Names the method only; the rates stay empty (see seedingRate.notRecorded). sownBy makes the crop planned by area with "Seed amount not known" instead of the 12 in placeholder spacing (panel ruling 2026-10-05, #576, 3-0 for area mode, 2-1 for a sourced marker over an empty seedingRate).

seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.quote: Mustard. Drill 5-12 lb./A ¼–¾ in. deep or broadcast 10-15 lb./A.
seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.note: Chart 3B agrees (drilled 5-12, broadcast 10-15). Generic mustard, not specific to the biofumigant line. The NRCS Iowa / Iowa State cover crop fact sheets (May 2025) print lower single pure-live-seed rates (rye 45 drilled and 50 broadcast, mustard 3 and 4). Seed basis alone cannot close a two- to three-fold gap; they are Midwest Cover Crops Council baseline rates for Iowa corn and soybean systems, and the rye sheet says 'If grazing or weed suppression is desired, increase seeding rate.' A different purpose and region, so not counted (panel ruling 2026-10-04). Maryland NRCS 340 (2025) prints winter rye 90 and mustard 8, inside these ranges.

seedingRate.notRecorded.publisher: SARE, Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Oats
seedingRate.notRecorded.quote: If drilling oats, seed at 2 to 3 bushels per acre 1/2 to 1 inch deep, or 1 1/2 inches when growing grain you plan to harrow for weed control.
seedingRate.notRecorded.note: Why every seeding rate is empty (panel ruling 2026-10-05, #551, 3-0): the crop page prints bushels only (drill 2-3 bu) and Chart 3B prints drilled 80-110 lb (2.5-3.5 bu) and broadcast 110-140 lb (3.5-4.5 bu), so the page and chart disagree and a lb figure would need a bushel weight no source prints. Other drilled figures: VCE 65-80, MD NRCS 340 95, PA NRCS 340 80, UGA C814 90-120, Kentucky AGR-18 '80 lb (drilled) 120 lb (broadcast)' pure live seed; Missouri G4652 90-120 (forage) and Ohio ANR-0116 30-60 (MCCC baseline) are not counted. No source prints a cover-crop drill row width (VCE's 6-8 in is the grain-oats sentence; panel split 2026-10-04). Penn State Agronomy Guide 2025 is paywalled and was not read.

keepApart.publisher: UMass Amherst Extension Vegetable Program, "Onion Thrips" fact sheet
keepApart.date: Page shows no publication date; accessed 2026-10-03
keepApart.quote: Avoid planting onions near alfalfa, wheat or clover, as these crops can harbor large populations of thrips.
keepApart.note: Agreeing sources: Utah State University Extension Vegetable Guide, Onion Thrips (https://extension.usu.edu/vegetableguide/onion/onion-thrips.php): "Avoid planting onion adjacent to alfalfa fields."; UC IPM Onion and Garlic Pest Management Guidelines, Thrips (https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/onion-and-garlic/thrips/): "Avoid planting onions near grain or alfalfa fields if possible, because thrips often increase in those fields in the spring and migrate to onion fields when the grain senesces, or when the alfalfa is cut."; University of Kentucky Entomology EF328 (https://Entomology.Ca.Uky.Edu/files/ef328.pdf): "Avoid planting near alfalfa and small grains if possible." Only bulb onion plugins are listed. Clover is left out because the sources name it only as "clover", not a species.

seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.publisher: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture, Orchardgrass for Forage (FSA3154)
seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.quote: Seeding rate: 10-12 lbs/acre drilled; 12-15 lbs broadcast
seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.note: Pure stand; the sheet lists Potomac among varieties that did well in Kentucky and Tennessee trials. Overlapping method-split sources: UGA Circular 814 'D: 10-15 lbs/A B: 15-20 lbs/A' and Missouri G4652 drilled 8-15 (pounds of live seed). VCE 424-100 and Penn State print 8-12 pure stand and Kentucky AGR-64 15-20, none naming a method, so they are not counted. Basis not stated, so no seedBasis. Broadcast is left empty: 12-15 here vs 15-20 in UGA C814 (panel ruling 2026-10-04). Broadcast stays empty permanently unless a source changes: a single shared endpoint (15) is a disagreement (panel ruling 2026-10-05, 2-1).

treeSizeClasses.dwarf.publisher: Virginia Cooperative Extension, Tree Fruit in the Home Garden, Publication 426-841 (Virginia Tech)
treeSizeClasses.dwarf.date: 2020-09-21 (publication date shown on the page; accessed 2026-10-05)
treeSizeClasses.dwarf.quote: VCE 426-841, Table 1, "Space requirement, yield, bearing age, and life expectancy of tree fruits", columns "Fruit | Minimum Distance Between Plants (feet) | Approximate Yield Per Plant (bushels) | Bearing Age (years) | Life Expectancy (years)"; row "Apple - dwarf | 8 | 2 | 2-3 | 30-35 |". Same page, on rootstocks: "the same variety of apple will produce a 16- to 18-foot tree on the rootstock Malling Merton (MM)111, down to a dwarf tree of 7 to 8 feet on a Malling (M)9 rootstock." and "Trees on M.9 rootstock will often produce crops in two to three years."
treeSizeClasses.dwarf.note: Panel ruling 2026-10-05 (#548), 2-1: VCE itself calls a tree on M.9 a dwarf, so this is VCE's apple dwarf row, the same row the five apple plugins carry. NC State Extension Gardener Handbook ch. 15 (https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/extension-gardener-handbook/15-tree-fruit-and-nuts) agrees on bearing age, Table 15-3 "M.9 | 35 | 20 | 2 – 3" (Fruit-Bearing Age (Years)), and its Table 15-4 recommended distance "M.9** | 4 – 8 | 3 – 5 | 6 – 11" (nonspur, spur, very vigorous cultivars) reaches 8 for nonspur cultivars; NC State's Production Guide for Smaller Orchard Plantings, Table 3, gives "M.9 and M.9 sized trees* | 4-8 | 3-5 | 6-8". Penn State Home Orchards Table 4.3 gives "Malling 9 | 35 | 3-5 x 12" (suggested spacing, ft) and Cornell's Guide to Growing Fruit at Home (New York, not used) "Apple, M.9 7 13 3-5"; the data-integrity panelist voted to ship nothing because those closer spacings depend on growth habit and do not overlap VCE's 8 ft minimum. harvestIndicators.quote: SARE, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, Sorghum-Sudangrass Hybrids: "Mowing or grazing when stalks are 3 to 4 feet tall encourages tillering and deeper root growth, and keeps regrowth vegetative and less fibrous until frost. seedingRate.broadcastLbsPerAcre.publisher: SARE, Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Sorghum-Sudangrass
seedingRate.broadcastLbsPerAcre.quote: With sufficient surface moisture, broadcast 40 to 50 lb./A, or drill 35 to 40 lb./A as deep as 2 inches to reach moist soil.
seedingRate.broadcastLbsPerAcre.note: Chart 3B agrees on broadcast 40-50. Smother-crop cover rates: the page says these rates give a quicker canopy than the lower rates used for forage. The NRCS Iowa / Iowa State fact sheet (May 2025) prints 15 drilled and 17 broadcast lb/acre PLS; seed basis alone cannot close a gap that size. It is an Iowa baseline for a different purpose, so it is not counted (panel ruling 2026-10-04).

seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.publisher: SARE, Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Sorghum-Sudangrass
seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.quote: With sufficient surface moisture, broadcast 40 to 50 lb./A, or drill 35 to 40 lb./A as deep as 2 inches to reach moist soil.
seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.note: Chart 3B prints a single 35, inside this range; the crop page's range is used (overlap rule, panel ruling 2026-10-04). Smother-crop cover rates: the page says these rates give a quicker canopy than the lower rates used for forage. The NRCS Iowa / Iowa State fact sheet (May 2025) prints 15 drilled and 17 broadcast lb/acre PLS; seed basis alone cannot close a gap that size. It is an Iowa baseline for a different purpose, so it is not counted (panel ruling 2026-10-04).

seedingRate.seedBasis.publisher: SARE, Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Charts
seedingRate.seedBasis.quote: Rate. Recommended seeding rate for drilling and broadcasting a pure stand in lb./A, bu/A. and oz./100 sq. ft., assuming legal standards for germination percentage. Seeding rate will depend on the cover crop’s primary purpose and other factors.
seedingRate.seedBasis.note: Seed as bought (labelled seed of legal germination), not pure live seed: shown as bulk seed (panel ruling 2026-10-04). The crop pages are the same book and give bushel equivalents, a bulk weight.

seedingRate.purpose.publisher: SARE, Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Sorghum-Sudangrass
seedingRate.purpose.quote: These rates provide a quicker canopy to smother weeds than lower rates used for forage production, but they require mowing or grazing to prevent lodging.
seedingRate.purpose.note: The sentence right after the rate sentence on the same page, so the purpose belongs to the shipped 35-40 drilled and 40-50 broadcast rates (panel ruling 2026-10-05, #576, 3-0). PA NRCS 340 prints 20 for an adequate single-species stand and says to raise it 25% when the purpose is weed suppression; 25 still does not overlap 35-40, so the label makes the shipped rate honest about its use, it does not make it agree with NRCS.

keepApart.publisher: NC State Extension (Lorena Lopez, "Tarnished Plant Bug in Strawberries")
keepApart.quote: Avoid locating strawberry fields immediately adjacent to alfalfa fields, large weedy areas, small-grain fields, or disturbed vegetation or other major TPB source habitats.
keepApart.note: Agreeing source: UNH Cooperative Extension, Alan T. Eaton and Rachel Maccini, "Tarnished Plant Bug" pest fact sheet (updated June 2016, https://extension.unh.edu/resources/files/Resource000555_Rep577.pdf): "Crop Placement - Avoid planting susceptible crops, such as strawberries, close to clover or alfalfa crops." The NC State page also describes alfalfa strips as a managed trap crop paired with vacuuming in California organic systems; that is a deliberate trap-crop system, not unmanaged neighbouring plantings, and the same page's cultural advice is to keep strawberries away from alfalfa. Clover and small grains are left out because the sources name them only generically.

inRowSpacingIn.quote: "Under the matted-row system used by many home gardeners, runner plants are allowed to set freely in all directions. The original plants should be set 18 to 24 inches apart in the row."

seasonalTasks.frost-watch.quote: University of Minnesota Extension, Protect strawberries from spring freeze and frost: "Once the blossoms are open, they are damaged at 30° F." Same page: "So this only works if water is continuously applied during the freezing period and until temperatures rise above freezing." and "Not applying enough water or stopping irrigation too early during a nighttime freeze, can cause more damage than not irrigating at all."
seasonalTasks.frost-watch.note: OP-20 panel 2026-10-05 (docs/design/ORCHARD_CALENDAR.md, table "OP-20 number rulings"). Q1 (2-1): 30 °F kept; overhead irrigation kept only with the UMN operating caveat. Agreeing sources: UMaine Highmoor Strawberry IPM Newsletter 2023-05-16 ("At the open blossom stage: 30 °F"), Cornell berry blog 2020-05-06 Table 1 (open blossom 30), NC State Strawberry Growers Information (critical temperature of 30 F). The irrigation start temperature is left out because the sources disagree (UMN below 34 °F, UMaine before freezing, NC State by wet bulb).

seasonalTasks.row-renovation.publisher: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach (Yard and Garden)
seasonalTasks.row-renovation.quote: Iowa State Yard and Garden, How do you renovate June-bearing strawberries?: "mowing off the leaves 1 inch above the crowns of the plants with a rotary mower within 1 week of the last harvest."
seasonalTasks.row-renovation.note: OP-20 panel 2026-10-05 (docs/design/ORCHARD_CALENDAR.md, table "OP-20 number rulings"). Q2 (2-1): "within 1 week" kept; UMN ("Renovation should start immediately after the end of harvest.") and VCE 426-840 ("soon after harvest (mid-July)") agree it starts right after harvest. The "narrow rows to 12 in" width was dropped because the sources disagree: Iowa State 8-to-12-inch strips, UMN as little as 6 inches growing to 12 to 14, VCE a 16 to 18 inch bed. seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.publisher: University of Missouri Extension G4652, Seeding Rates, Dates and Depths for Common Missouri Forages (Harley D. Naumann)
seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.quote: Missouri G4652 Table 1. Pure stands, columns "Type | Seeding rate (pounds of live seed per acre) | Seeding date (Spring, Fall, Dormant or frost seeding) | Depth"; row "Timothy Perennial, cool-season grass Drilled: 4 – 6 Broadcast: 8 – 10 February – March Mid-August – early September 1/4 – 1/2 inch"
seedingRate.drilledLbsPerAcre.note: Forage pure-stand rate; the plugin is a hay timothy, so it counts (panel ruling 2026-10-05, #551). Kentucky AGR-84 Timothy, the crop guide, gives the same 'plant at the rate of 4 to 6 lb of seed per acre' for pure stands, in the paragraph on tilled seedbeds and no-till drilling. VCE 424-100 ('8-10 lbs alone'), Kentucky AGR-18 and Tennessee give 8-10 or 8 with no method, so they do not count. Missouri says 'live seed' but not 'pure live seed', so no seedBasis is set.

seedingRate.drillRowSpacingIn.note: Crop guide; single source for the drill row width (panel ruling 2026-10-05, #551, 3-0).

seedingRate.broadcastLbsPerAcre.publisher: USDA NRCS Plant Guide, Japanese millet (Echinochloa esculenta)
seedingRate.broadcastLbsPerAcre.quote: It can be broadcast at 20 lb/ac and covered lightly ¼ in deep for wildlife food planting (Stewart and West, 2004) or directly seeded into mud flats or well-prepared fields.
seedingRate.broadcastLbsPerAcre.note: Crop guide's single figure; UGA C814 (broadcast 20-25) and Kentucky AGR-18 ('20 lb (broadcast)', pure live seed) contain it (panel ruling 2026-10-05, #551, 3-0). seedingRate.seedsPerAcre.publisher: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension AGR-18, Grain, Forage, and Cover Crop Guide for Kentucky
seedingRate.seedsPerAcre.quote: Kentucky AGR-18 table, columns "Species Scientific Name | Uses | Common Units | Desired Plant Density | Seeding Rate Pure Live Seed/ac | Seeding Depth (inches)"; row "Sorghum, Grain (Milo) Sorghum bicolor | grain | 56 lb/bu 24,000 seeds/lb | 60,000/ac | 60,000 to 80,000 seeds | 3/4 to 1-1/4"

Single source; nothing disagrees (panel ruling 2026-10-05, #551, 3-0). The lb rate stays empty: VCE 424-100 'Plant for grain at 5-7 lbs in rows' (wide rows, not a drill) and UGA C814 D 6-8, and University of Delaware Weekly Crop Update (May 16, 2008) says 'Do not plant using the older suggestions of pounds per acre since grain sorghum seed size has varied from almost 8,000 seed per pound up to 18,000 seed per pound.' Row width stays empty: Delaware's 7-10 in and AGR-18's '15" or less' compare yield and lodging, they do not recommend a width.

seedingRate.notRecorded.publisher: University of Maryland Extension FS-1134, No-Till Spring Vegetables After Forage Radish Cover Crop
seedingRate.notRecorded.quote: Recommended seeding rates for the popular Tillage Radish brand are 6 lbs/acre drilled, though research trials at the University of Maryland generally used a higher seeding rate of 8-9 lbs/acre. Broadcast rates are higher (9-12 lbs/acre)

The brand owner (DLF / La Crosse Seed) prints 'Seeding Rate - Alone/New (Lbs./Acre) 3-8' with no method, so it does not count.

Also read: https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/files/2023/12/A1960.pdf (10-12 ft, overlaps); https://extension.oregonstate.edu/node/210886 (12-13 ft, overlaps).

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: Utah State University Extension

rowSpacingIn.publisher: Oregon State University Extension Service

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: Utah State University Extension
inRowSpacingIn.quote: USU Extension, Haskap in the Garden, Planting and Spacing: "For most cultivars, leaving 3 to 4 feet between plants within the row and 6 to 10 feet between rows is sufficient."
inRowSpacingIn.note: Generic haskap figure applied to Aurora. No mid-Atlantic source found.

rowSpacingIn.publisher: USDA NRCS Plant Materials Program (Plant Fact Sheet, Corvallis Plant Materials Center)

The fact sheet covers A. alnifolia var. semiintegrifolia (Pacific serviceberry); Saskatoon is the same species (the USU serviceberry page I read gives no row figure). Written for conservation/seedling plantings, not fruit orchards. Feet converted to inches; lower end of the between-row figure (#591 ruling Q1).

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: USDA NRCS Plant Materials Program (Plant Fact Sheet)
inRowSpacingIn.quote: USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet, Saskatoon serviceberry (Amelanchier alnifolia): "Seedlings may be planted in rows; between row and within row spacing should be a minimum of 12 feet and 6 feet, respectively."

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: NC State Extension (North Carolina State University)

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: UF/IFAS Extension (University of Florida)
inRowSpacingIn.date: HS-867/HS132; no publication date printed in the fetched page (page © 2024) (accessed 2026-10-06)
inRowSpacingIn.quote: UF/IFAS EDIS HS-867/HS132, Citrus Culture in the Home Landscape: "For home plantings, the spacing recommended should be a minimum of 15 feet between trees."; "The 'Meyer' lemon is a reasonable substitute for true lemons in home gardens."
inRowSpacingIn.note: Between-TREE figure (minimum spacing between trees; tree group), not between rows. Single minimum figure for in-ground citrus in Florida home plantings; applies to all citrus, Meyer lemon included. In Loudoun County, VA, Meyer lemon is not winter-hardy outdoors and would normally be grown in a container, where a planting distance does not apply. Feet converted to inches; replaces an unsourced range (#591).

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: Oregon State University Extension Service
inRowSpacingIn.quote: OSU EM 9077, Growing Hazelnuts in the Pacific Northwest: Orchard Design, Spacing and Arrangement of Permanent Trees: "The standard 20 × 20-foot square (6 × 6 meters) with 108 trees per acre (267 trees per hectare) is adaptable to a variety of soils and situations."; "For well-managed orchards with good soils, an 18 × 18-foot square (5.5 × 5.5 meters) with 134 trees per acre (331 trees per hectare) is a good permanent spacing for some soils and varieties."
inRowSpacingIn.note: Between-TREE figure (minimum spacing between trees; tree group), not between rows. Square orchard spacing (same distance between trees in and across rows); permanent spacing 18-20 ft. The pub also describes temporary double-density 10 x 20 ft layouts thinned later. Jefferson is an Oregon State release, so this PNW source fits the cultivar; not a home-garden or mid-Atlantic source. NC State Table 15-5 and VCE 426-841 do not list hazelnut. Feet converted to inches; replaces an unsourced range (#591).

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: NC State Extension (North Carolina State University)
inRowSpacingIn.date: Extension Gardener Handbook AG-831, Publication date: Feb. 1, 2022 (accessed 2026-10-06)
inRowSpacingIn.quote: NC State Extension Gardener Handbook, Chapter 15 Tree Fruit and Nuts, Table 15–5 (Fruit Crop | Minimum Spacing Between Trees (feet)): "Fruit Crop | Minimum Spacing Between Trees (feet) |"; "Chestnuts | 40 |"
inRowSpacingIn.note: Minimum distance between trees, feet converted to inches. VCE ANR-279P, Commercial Chinese Chestnut Production in Virginia (https://accomack.ext.vt.edu/content/dam/pubs_ext_vt_edu/ANR/ANR-279/ANR-279.pdf), agrees: "If minimizing labor is desired, chestnut trees should be planted at a 40-by-40-foot spacing" (its 20-30 ft layout is thinned to every other tree around year 15). inRowSpacingIn.publisher: Utah State University Extension
inRowSpacingIn.quote: USU Extension, How to Grow Walnuts in Your Yard, Spacing: "For the home orchard, space trees 30 to 50 feet apart."; "Carpathian type English walnuts are a better choice for most areas of Utah due to improved winter hardiness"
inRowSpacingIn.note: Between-TREE figure (minimum spacing between trees; tree group), not between rows. The spacing line covers walnuts generally; the page discusses Carpathian English walnuts by name. NC State Table 15-5 lists only Black Walnut (10-12 ft), a different species, so it was not used. No VCE or mid-Atlantic English walnut spacing found. Feet converted to inches; replaces an unsourced range (#591).

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources (UC Master Gardener Program of Sonoma County)
inRowSpacingIn.quote: UC ANR Sonoma County Master Gardeners, Rapini (Broccoli Raab): "For the home gardener, plant or thin to six-inches apart, so that plants can develop a good quantity of greens. Pulled seedlings transplant well and can be moved to another row, if desired."
inRowSpacingIn.note: Generic rapini figure applied to Sorrento. Final spacing after thinning; the sentence gives plant-to-plant distance in a row-planted crop but does not say "in the row". No VCE, UMD or Mid-Atlantic in-row figure found: VCE 426-403 only refers raab to 426-408, whose spacings are unlabelled "X x Y"; the NC State "Broccoli Raab" page is withdrawn. The old Cornell growing guide (the same source: "Thin to 4 to 6 inches apart.", overlaps 6) is served over http only, so it is not allowed. A UC Master Gardener county page is weaker than a state extension publication.

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: University of Florida IFAS Extension (HS1370, Daikon Radish Cultivation Guide for Florida)
inRowSpacingIn.quote: UF/IFAS HS1370, Daikon Radish Cultivation Guide for Florida: "Culture is quite similar to that of the common radish (R. sativus) with the exception of plant spacing, which should be 4–6 inches in rows spaced 3 ft apart"
inRowSpacingIn.note: UF HS1370 is daikon-specific, so it is reported as the main figure even though UMD (mid-Atlantic) ranks higher: UMD gives one 2-4 in range across spring, daikon and winter types; it overlaps UF at 4 in. VCE 426-331 "Radish" is spring radish (no overlap). The Mid-Atlantic manual gives radishes as 12-15 plants/ft (a density, not a distance).

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: University of Maryland Extension (Home and Garden Information Center)
inRowSpacingIn.quote: UMD Extension, Growing Radishes in the Home Garden: "Spacing: Plant seeds 1 - 2 inches apart in-rows and ¼ - ½ inch deep, or equidistantly in wide rows or beds, depending on the variety."; "When they germinate, thin the seedlings so that the remaining plants are 2 to 4 inches apart depending on the type."; "There are several types of radishes- small spring, Asian daikon, and winter storage cultivars."
inRowSpacingIn.note: Not an exact match: watermelon radish is a Chinese winter radish; UMD gives one 2-4 in final range "depending on the type" across spring, daikon and winter types, so the larger end likely applies. VCE 426-331 "Radish" is spring radish (no overlap). UF daikon 4-6 in overlaps at 4 (a related but different winter radish).

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: Utah State University Extension
inRowSpacingIn.quote: USU Extension, How to Grow Watercress in Your Garden, Planting and Spacing: "When transplanting, space plants 8 inches apart and place them outdoors after the last frost."
inRowSpacingIn.note: Exact crop match. Single figure; distance between plants (no row axis is given, the page does not describe rows). Watercress is aquatic/saturated-soil; the figure is for transplants. No mid-Atlantic source found.

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: NC State Extension (North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox)

inRowSpacingIn.note: Garden plant-to-plant spacing ("planted 12 to 36 inches apart"); no row named. Not in VCE 426-420 or the UCANR herb table; the UMD anise-hyssop/agastache URLs cached in #591 are 404 pages. The toolbox Width field (1 ft 6 in - 3 ft) is plant size, not spacing.

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach (Yard and Garden)
inRowSpacingIn.quote: ISU Yard and Garden, Growing Bee Balm in the Home Garden: "When planting bee balms, select a site in full sun and space plants 2 feet apart."
inRowSpacingIn.note: 2 ft = 24 in, plant-to-plant (no row named). Generic bee balm (Monarda) applied to M. didyma. No VCE/mid-Atlantic figure found: UMD HGIC bee balm/monarda URLs are 404; Penn State rain-garden bee balm, UMD Maryland Grows, UGA Field Report, Illinois and NC State Plant Toolbox give no spacing (toolbox Width is plant size); Clemson HGIC blocked by Cloudflare.

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: Mississippi State University Extension Service, Snapdragon (Antirrhinum majus) for the Farmer Florist, Publication 3301
inRowSpacingIn.quote: MSU Extension Publication 3301, Snapdragon (Antirrhinum majus) for the Farmer Florist: "Plants should be spaced 4–12 inches apart."
inRowSpacingIn.note: Not counted (no axis): UMass annuals (the same source, names the Rocket series) "Snapdragons can be spaced 8x8\""; Cornell High Tunnels "4 x 4 in." / "9 x 9 in.". No mid-Atlantic source with a labelled figure found.

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: University of Maryland, Department of Horticulture (Dr. William E. Healy and Ignacio Espinosa), "Producing Cut Flowers - Florist Statice", Minnesota Flower Growers Bulletin Vol. 40 No. 1 (reprinted from The Flower Market 2(12):6-8); scan hosted by NC State Extension
inRowSpacingIn.quote: Healy and Espinosa (UMD), Producing Cut Flowers - Florist Statice, Field Plant Spacing: "Grow two to three rows of statice plants per bed, and space the plants 12 to 14 inches apart across the bed (alternate space), and 14 to 16 inches apart down the bed."
inRowSpacingIn.note: "Down the bed" is the along-the-row direction in a 2-3 row bed (12-14 in is across the bed). Maryland trials (mid-Atlantic). Seen but not allowed: USU "Statice Cut Flower Production" copy on projects.sare.org (the same source, .org host) "Space plants 8 to 12 inches apart" - would not overlap 14-16; LSU AgCenter article (the same source, .com host) "Seedlings can be planted 12 inches apart in a single drill line" - would not overlap. Cornell High Tunnels statice "12 x 12 in." is unlabelled.

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: Utah State University Extension, Strawflower Cut Flower Production in Utah
inRowSpacingIn.quote: USU Extension, Strawflower Cut Flower Production in Utah, Transplanting and Spacing: "Space plants 9 to 12 inches apart to avoid overcrowding at maturity; USU trials used 12-inch spacing."
inRowSpacingIn.note: Seen but not allowed: LSU AgCenter cut-flower guide (the same source, .com host) "12" spacing" (unlabelled; would overlap). No mid-Atlantic source found.

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: Colorado State University Extension
inRowSpacingIn.date: Fact sheet 7.005, Published: October 1999, Reviewed: August 2025 (accessed 2026-10-06)
inRowSpacingIn.quote: Colorado State Extension 7.005, Currants, Gooseberries, and Jostaberries, Planting: "Plant them 3.5 to 4.5 feet apart in early spring, in rows spaced 6 to 8 feet apart."; "Jostaberry is a fast-growing hybrid between the black currant and gooseberry."
inRowSpacingIn.note: The fact sheet covers currants, gooseberries and jostaberries together; "them" in the planting sentence refers to all three (jostaberry is named in the title and throughout), so this figure covers jostaberry itself, not a parent crop. Not mid-Atlantic. Checked without a jostaberry figure: Univ. of Minnesota currant/gooseberry page (jostaberry described; spacing given only for currants/gooseberries), Oregon State EM 9182, Penn State. Seed-company/nursery pages (T&T Seeds, Gurney's, Stark Bros) are not allowed.

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: University of Florida IFAS Extension (EDIS; archived copy on EDIS journal, journals.flvc.org)
inRowSpacingIn.quote: UF/IFAS HS568, Burdock — Arctium lappa L., Culture: "The seeds germinate readily and should be sown in rows 18 inches apart in late fall or early spring (all winter in South Florida). Thin the seedlings to stand 6 inches apart in the row."
inRowSpacingIn.note: Final spacing after thinning (6 in). Generic edible burdock figure applied to Takinogawa Long. Kansas State MF2609 'Burdock' was the other candidate (a search excerpt says 'at least 18 inches apart'), but the K-State bookstore serves it only through a script-driven download page that curl cannot retrieve, so it was not read or counted. Purdue NewCROP 'Burdock, Edible' was blocked by Purdue's firewall; hawaii.edu exotic-crops page is http only.

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: University of Minnesota Extension
inRowSpacingIn.quote: UMN Extension, Growing tomatillos and ground cherries in home gardens: "Allow ground cherry plants 18 to 24 inches of space in all directions."
inRowSpacingIn.note: 'in all directions' is equidistant spacing, so it includes the distance between plants in the row. Generic ground cherry figure applied to Aunt Molly's (Physalis pruinosa). DISAGREEMENT (unclear): Penn State prints 'four 4 apart' with no unit.

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: N.C. Cooperative Extension (NC State University)
inRowSpacingIn.quote: NC State Extension, Cultivation of Ramps (Allium tricoccum and A. burdickii), Transplanting: "transplant the bulbs approximately 3 inches deep, and 4 to 6 inches apart"; "Transplant leafed-out plants at the same depth they had been growing and space 4 to 6 inches apart."
inRowSpacingIn.note: Plant-to-plant spacing in a prepared bed or woodland planting; NC State names no rows, so the figure is the distance between plants (equals in-row spacing for bed planting). The same page says clumps of 4 or 5 plants can be grouped together if space is limited. No second allowed source found.

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: University of Vermont, North American Center for Saffron Research and Development
inRowSpacingIn.quote: UVM, Saffron planting for home gardeners (Sept. 2021): "Corms should be planted at a density of 6-12 corms per sq. ft, usually around 3-4 inches apart."
inRowSpacingIn.note: Corm-to-corm spacing in beds or crates (density 6-12 corms per sq ft); no rows named, so the figure is the distance between plants. The UVM 'home gardeners' PDF matches the #591 cache the same source byte for byte (re-fetched 2026-10-06).

inRowSpacingIn.publisher: University of Florida IFAS Extension (EDIS)
inRowSpacingIn.quote: UF/IFAS HS1435, Yacon, a Potential Tuberous Crop for Florida: "rooted stem cuttings or plants propagated from corms can be planted in beds with 3- or 4-foot center-to-center spacing (Chqoue Delago et al. 2013) with 30–40 inches for plant spacing (Herman and Heller 1997)."
inRowSpacingIn.note: 'plant spacing' within beds (beds 3-4 ft center to center) is read as the distance between plants along the bed. The figure is cited from Herman and Heller 1997 rather than a UF trial. No other allowed yacon source found (other hits were journal articles).

seedingRate.seedsPerAcre.publisher: NC State Extension, North Carolina Soybean Production Guide (AG-835), 5. Planting Decisions
seedingRate.seedsPerAcre.quote: In planting situations earlier than mid-May, soybean seeding rates of 120,000 to 150,000 seeds/acre generally maximized yield, while with later planting dates (past mid-June), seeding rates of 165,000 to 175,000 seeds/acre were needed to maximize yield.
seedingRate.seedsPerAcre.note: #689. Seeds per acre for a full-season planting before mid-May, the usual Virginia planting for a group 3.5 bean (VCE 424-100 Soybean: two weeks after corn planting time, prior to June 10). Double-crop or late plantings need more seed (165,000 to 175,000 past mid-June, same sentence), which the plugin cannot express, so the full-season figure is stored. VCE 424-100 (2023) Part I Soybean was read and gives no seeding rate; the Virginia Tech soybean blog posts that gave one are no longer online, so no Virginia figure was counted.
